subject: biology
title: Calculating Magnification
welcome_lead: Turn a small image into a giant one using simple multiplication of lens powers.
meta_desc: KS3 Biology adventure on calculating microscope magnification.
final_note: You can now work out total magnification from the lenses you choose.

concepts.def: How many times bigger something looks.
Lower lens, e.g. x4, x10, x40.
Circle of sample you can see.
How clear or detailed the image is.

walkthroughs.body_html: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective. If the eyepiece is x10 and the objective is x40, total is x400.
Use a low objective to find your sample. Switch to a higher objective for fine detail. The field of view becomes smaller but you see more detail.
Eyepiece x10, objective x4 → total x40. Eyepiece x10, objective x10 → total x100. Eyepiece x10, objective x40 → total x400.

mcqs.q: Where does transcription occur in a eukaryotic cell?
options: In the nucleus — DNA is transcribed to mRNA, which then travels to the cytoplasm.
Frameshift mutations are usually silent because cells can correct them.
Transcription happens in mitochondria where ATP is produced.

mcqs.q: Why are frameshift mutations usually more severe than point substitutions?
options: Frameshifts only change the codon at the site of the mutation, like a substitution.
Frameshift mutations are usually silent because cells can correct them.
The entire DNA sequence of every individual changes simultaneously.
Insertions/deletions of a non-multiple of 3 shift the reading frame, changing every codon downstream of the mutation.

mcqs.q: What actually changes during natural selection in a population?
options: Frameshift mutations are usually silent because cells can correct them.
The frequencies of alleles in the population's gene pool change across generations.
Individual organisms change their own genes to adapt.
The entire DNA sequence of every individual changes simultaneously.
